CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

2 of 3 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 0 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen (glycoCEST): ✓ detectable (both)
  • Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT): ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Glutamine: ✗ not detectable

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (GAG): present only in small amounts in normal liver (perisinusoidal Ito/fat-storing cells) and markedly elevated only in fibrosis/cirrhosis (PMID 1381623, 3095167, 3151542). Normal liver is not GAG-rich as cartilage is, so no normal-tissue >1 mM disaccharide-unit number and gagCEST is not a robust normal-liver target.; [model's own exclusion] Taurine: excluded because it is a constituent of bile (a secreted fluid), not a species stored in the liver parenchyma, so it is not a CEST target of the liver tissue itself (PMID 401099, 36988554).; [model's own exclusion] Glutamate (Glu): a known hepatocyte pool overlapping the Gln/Glu MRS peak (PMID 17128381, 11859290) with exchangeable protons, but no explicit >1 mM tissue-stored concentration number was directly obtained; not estimated to avoid fabrication.; [model's own exclusion] Alanine (Ala): a major liver metabolite with exchangeable protons, but no direct >1 mM tissue-stored number surfaced in the searches.; [model's own exclusion] ATP/ADP/AMP: high-energy phosphate pool with exchangeable protons (PMID 2444209), but no direct mM tissue value obtained and primarily 31P-observable.; [model's own exclusion] Creatine/creatine phosphate: not a major stored liver metabolite; no liver number found.; [model's own exclusion] Bile acids / taurine-conjugated bile acids (PMID 31571251, 32020463): secreted into bile, i.e. a secretion rather than a stored parenchymal pool, so not a CEST target of the liver tissue itself.

Glycogen (glycoCEST) — CEST: ✓ detectable (both)

Concentration: 323.00 mM typical (roughly 0 (fasted) to ~323 mM glucosyl-equivalent (fed rat liver); human fed-liver values typically in the tens of mM)

Show literature excerpt supporting this concentration — PMID 3429768
“Rat liver tissue contained a mean 323 +/- 69 mmol of glucose equivalents of glycogen per gram of tissue; this glycogen had a mean chain length of 11.4 +/- 0.8 units.”

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners:

  • Contrast over the uncertainty corners (hydroxyl OH (C2, C3, C4, C6 alcohols of glucosyl unit) [hydroxyl]: concentration 0-323 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); glycoNOE aliphatic C-H (ring C2-C5 H and CH2OH C6 protons, glucosyl unit) [rnoe]: concentration 0-323 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-1.83%, 1.5 T: 0.00-2.98%, 3 T: 0.00-4.93%, 5 T: 0.00-7.14%, 7 T: 0.00-8.01%.
  • Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • 0.5 T: OH at +1.00 ppm is 53 Hz from APT amide and 96 Hz from APT-rNOE against a ~5100 Hz linewidth -- total blur; the 1.8% cannot be attributed to OH alone. 1.5 T: glycoNOE at -1.1 ppm is 83 Hz from the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm), linewidth ~15940 Hz -- heavy MT contamination.
  • 3 T: 166 Hz from MT, still overlapped. 5 T: 277 Hz, borderline. 7 T: 387 Hz, resolves but with a long MT tail.
  • Self-collision OH (+1.0) vs glycoNOE (-1.1): 2.1 ppm gap = 167 Hz at 1.5 T (blurred, OH linewidth ~5100 Hz), 540 Hz at 3 T, 1245 Hz at 7 T -- the two glycogen features separate only at 3 T+. APT amide is clean from both glycogen pools at 3 T+.

Direct water saturation: Direct-saturation bandwidth is 10.6 Hz at all fields. OH (+1.0 ppm) is 43 Hz from water at 0.5 T (marginally outside), 129 Hz at 1.5 T, 258 Hz at 3 T, 430 Hz at 5 T, 602 Hz at 7 T. glycoNOE (-1.1 ppm) is 47 Hz at 0.5 T, 142 Hz at 1.5 T, and farther at higher fields. Direct saturation does not mask either pool at any field. The dominant contamination is MT (upfield), not direct water spillover.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • OH kex 31850 s-1 is from a PHANTOM / glycogen solution at 37 C (PMID 38933551), derived via Swift-Connick from R2, not a CEST measurement pH and field unstated provenance states 'borrowed from phantom, mouse, no liver-specific measurement.' Solution sugar-OH exchange is strongly pH/crowding-dependent and may differ from in-vivo liver by 2-10x
  • 31850 s-1 is fast enough that the simulation flags 0.5 T OH as 'fast exchange, direct saturation dominates.' The glycoNOE k_eff = 5 s-1 is a CLASS-LEVEL rNOE rate from a protein phantom (PMID 25996515), not measured for glycogen in liver, and the -1.1 ppm shift is from mouse muscle, not liver.
  • Treat all glycogen contrast as an upper-bound estimate, not a prediction.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.826% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — glycoNOE k_eff 5 s-1 is slow exchange; the CEST transfer function peaks at low B1 and broadens with B1, so 0.25 µT is optimal (higher B1 blurs the -1.1 ppm dip into the -2.4 ppm MT pool and the direct-saturation tail). Tsat 2 s needed to reach steady state for a 5 s-1 transfer process.
    recommended sequence: 2.980% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow-exchange physics unchanged; 3000 ms Tsat compensates for longer T1 and slower approach to steady state at higher B0 where offset in Hz grows but kex is unchanged. 0.25 µT keeps the glycoNOE dip narrow enough to partially resolve from the MT shoulder. Multi-pool fitting essential.
    recommended sequence: 4.935% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 5 T the -1.1 ppm dip is 473 Hz from water and 277 Hz from MT; Hz separation from MT has grown, but the sweep kept 0.25 µT, indicating the optimum is set by MT overlap, not direct saturation. 3 s Tsat for steady state.
    recommended sequence: 7.143% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — 387 Hz from MT at 7 T is the best field for resolving glycoNOE from the MT tail. 0.25 µT and 3 s Tsat are the sweep optimum; higher B1 would improve transfer but blur the dip into MT, so the physics optimum stays low. Multi-pool quantitative CEST (QUASS-type) is the right readout.
    recommended sequence: 8.008% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • Swept B1 = 0.25 µT at all fields, Tsat = 2-3 s, sits in the slow-exchange, low-B1 regime for the glycoNOE (k_eff 5 s-1). AREX is the preferred extraction here: it divides by the B1^2-normalized saturation profile, removing the T1 and direct-saturation bias that dominates at low B1.
  • Simple MTRasym at -1.1 ppm is contaminated by the -2.4 ppm MT pool and by abdominal B1 inhomogeneity. Multi-pool Lorentzian difference (QUASS-type, per PMID 42076810) is the rigorous alternative, requiring dense Z-spectrum sampling (41-53 offsets per PMID 26334509/36161668). Omega-plot exchange fitting is misapplied because the rNOE rate is not a true chemical-exchange rate.
  • The 3 T in-vivo liver data (PMID 26334509) used B0/B1-corrected MTRasym, a reasonable first approximation but not a clean glycoNOE measurement.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

glycogen (glycoCEST, MTRasym ~1.0 ppm / integrated 0.5-1.5 ppm): 2 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 11 animals; 5 dropped by verification). GlycoCEST (liver glycogen) has direct CEST evidence in human and rat liver across healthy fasting/feeding states and CCl4 intoxication, with the signal dropping in fasted or injured livers. Metabolite-change evidence (13C-MRS, T1 mapping) shows glycogen concentration and synthesis flux change with feeding, in healthy children/adults, and in IDDM. No disease-specific glycoCEST tumor or steatosis CEST study was found yet; the strongest link is healthy metabolic modulation.

Caveats / critique (10 points, 446 words) — Concentration 323 mM monomer-equivalent is a defensible mid-range post-prandial value; peak human liver glycogen can approach ~500-1000 mM but fasted liver is c…
  • Concentration 323 mM monomer-equivalent is a defensible mid-range post-prandial value; peak human liver glycogen can approach ~500-1000 mM but fasted liver is closer to 30-110 mM. 323 mM is an upper bound for a fasted state. The 0-323 mM range correctly encodes the fasted zero. Not a wrong number, but the simulated contrast is a post-prandial ceiling.
  • Both groups defensible in class. OH (4 aliphatic hydroxyls, hydroxyl class, intermediate exchange) is correct; the chemist's 0.5 ppm estimate is in the right region and the simulated 1.0 ppm matches the in-vivo liver window (0.5-1.5 ppm). The glycoNOE (rnoe, 7 C-H per glucosyl unit) class is correct.
  • No exchangeable protons neglected: glycosidic O is not a proton donor; the anomeric C1-H is among the 7 C-H. Minor: the four OH have different pKa, so the 1 ppm dip is actually broadened/multi-peaked rather than a single Lorentzian; the class assignment still holds.
  • OH: in-vivo human liver CEST integrates 0.5-1.5 ppm (PMID 36161668, 26334509, 26391991); simulation used 1.0 ppm, consistent. No discrepancy. glycoNOE: in-vivo shift -1.0/-1.2 ppm from mouse muscle (PMID 39529314, 42076810); simulation used -1.1 ppm. No in-vivo liver measurement of the glycoNOE offset exists; the mouse-muscle shift is a reasonable but unverified proxy for liver.
  • The rNOE dip in liver is implied by wide negative-offset Z-spectra but never isolated in a cited liver study. None. All exchangeable protons (4 OH) and the relevant non-exchangeable C-H rNOE pool (7) are accounted for. The carboxyl-free sugar has no additional exchangeable groups.

The exchangeable-proton groups below are still the chemist's own analysis and may have been reasoned from the wrong structure. Reported in glucosyl-unit mM (glucose-equivalents), the unit relevant for CEST simulation. An internal glucosyl unit of glycogen carries 3 exchangeable hydroxyl protons (C2-OH, C3-OH, C4-OH); the C6-OH is substituted in the glycosidic linkage.
  • Strongly meal/fasting dependent, zoned to perivenous hepatocytes (PMID 2891351, 3062788).

Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT) — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 100.00 mM typical (order-of-magnitude estimate only; the mobile (non-immobilized) amide pool is a small fraction of the ~70 g/100 g liver protein content, plausibly tens to ~100 mM in amide units; no direct mM value obtained)

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: This is an ESTIMATE, not a measured value. The APTw CEST peak in human and rat liver is well established and reproducible (PMID 26334509, 26391991, 30856541), confirming a substantial mobile amide pool. No direct mM value for the mobile amide pool in liver was found in the searches, so it is estimated from the liver protein mass fraction. Liver is ~70 g protein per 100 g wet tissue (reference-work level). Converting to molar amide units and taking the small mobile (non-immobilized) fraction gives an order-of-magnitude tens-to-~100 mM. Treated strictly as a back-of-envelope estimate to flag order of magnitude, not a precise number.

  • The APT amide is the best-resolved downfield peak at 3 T+, consistent with in-vivo literature.

Direct water saturation:

  • Direct-saturation bandwidth 21.3 Hz (0.5-1.5 T), 31.9 Hz (3-7 T). APT amide at 3.5 ppm is 150 Hz from water at 0.5 T, 451 Hz at 1.5 T, 902 Hz at 3 T, 1503 Hz at 5 T, 2105 Hz at 7 T -- all well clear. APT rNOE at -3.5 ppm is the same distance from water.
  • Direct saturation is not a limiting factor for APT at any field strength. The dominant contamination is MT (upfield, for the rNOE) and, at low field, spectral blur with glycoCEST.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • APT amide kex 65.5 s-1 is the median of 116 s-1 (human brain, PMID 40228056) and 15 s-1 (in vivo n=7, PMID 23008121). Provenance: 'no liver-specific exchange-rate measurement -- borrowed from brain, human.' The spread is 15-158 s-1.
  • This is the central weakness: liver protein composition (albumin, hemoglobin, metabolic enzymes) differs from brain, and local pH, ionic strength, and macromolecular crowding in hepatocytes differ from neurons.
  • The in-vivo APT MTRasym values in liver (PMID 26334509: ~2.4% in fed rat at 3 T) are consistent with a kex in the 20-100 s-1 range, so 65.5 s-1 is plausible but unverified. APT rNOE k_eff = 5 s-1 is a class-level protein phantom value (PMID 25996515), no liver-specific or even in-vivo measurement.
  • Treat the rNOE contrast (0.48-1.97%) as an order-of-magnitude estimate.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — APT amide contrast 0.51% just above threshold. kex ~65 s-1 is intermediate exchange; 750 ms Tsat is short enough to limit SAR and motion sensitivity. At 0.5 T the APT amide is 150 Hz from water, outside the 21.3 Hz direct-saturation band. However, 53 Hz separation from glycoCEST OH and 126 Hz from MT mean the 0.5 T APT is a composite feature. Use only as a composite CEST metric, not a specific APT measurement.
    recommended sequence: 0.506% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Contrast 1.53%. Sweep kept B1 at 0.5 µT but extended Tsat to 3 s. In the intermediate-exchange regime, APT contrast peaks at moderate B1; 0.5 µT is optimal because higher B1 would broaden the 3.5 ppm dip into the MT shoulder. 3 s Tsat needed to reach steady state and accumulate enough transfer for 1.5% contrast. Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting required to separate APT from MT and glycoCEST.
    recommended sequence: 1.532% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Contrast 2.30%, matching in-vivo rat liver APTw ~2.4% (PMID 26334509). Sweep raised B1 to 0.75 µT at 3 T. In intermediate exchange, optimal B1 scales roughly as sqrt(kex x delta_omega); at 3 T the offset is 902 Hz vs 300 Hz at 1 T, so optimal B1 shifts up. 0.75 µT is the sweep optimum. 3 s Tsat for steady state. This is the clinically relevant field; in-vivo literature is all at 3 T. B1-corrected MTRasym or multi-pool fitting is the standard readout.
    recommended sequence: 2.302% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Contrast 3.22%. Same B1 as 3 T; sweep did not raise B1 further, suggesting the 0.75 µT optimum is set by the exchange regime rather than the offset. 3 s Tsat. APT amide is 1503 Hz from water and 1256 Hz from MT -- well resolved. Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting recommended to handle residual MT tail.
    recommended sequence: 3.222% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Contrast 3.58%, the highest in the APT series. B1 stays at 0.75 µT -- sweep found no benefit to increasing B1, consistent with the intermediate-exchange optimum being set by kex rather than delta_omega at this point. 3 s Tsat. At 7 T the APT amide is 2105 Hz from water and 1758 Hz from MT -- the best-resolved field for APT. Multi-pool quantitative CEST is the appropriate readout; simple MTRasym would work but would not remove the MT contribution.
    recommended sequence: 3.576% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • Swept B1 = 0.5-0.75 µT, Tsat = 0.75-3 s, sits in the intermediate-exchange regime (kex ~65 s-1). This is the classic APT regime. The appropriate extraction is multi-pool Lorentzian difference (fit water + semisolid MT + APT amide + APT rNOE + glycoCEST simultaneously) or AREX (divide by B1^2-scaled water saturation profile).
  • Simple MTRasym at 3.5 ppm is the method used in the in-vivo liver literature (PMID 36161668, 26334509, 26391991, 32785767) and is adequate for a first approximation, but it includes a small MT contribution and is sensitive to B1 inhomogeneity (a real problem in the abdomen). The in-vivo studies all applied B0 and B1 correction to the MTRasym.
  • For the rNOE at -3.5 ppm, multi-pool Lorentzian fitting is essential because the rNOE dip sits on top of the MT pool. Omega-plot exchange-rate fitting (multiple B1 powers) is the most rigorous for extracting APT amide kex but is rarely done in liver due to scan time. The standard liver CEST literature uses single-B1 MTRasym with correction, a reasonable compromise.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

amide proton transfer (APT, MTRasym/APTw at 3.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 16 animals; 3 dropped by verification). The liver amide (APT) pool has the strongest CEST evidence of the three candidates: APTw/APT-SI is higher in HCC (human TACE-prediction model, AUC 0.851; rodent HCC xenografts) and is reduced by effective therapy; APT-CEST also tracks healthy fasting/feeding and rat CCl4/fasting liver injury. No APT CEST study in cirrhosis/fibrosis or steatosis surfaced. APT is well established as a tumor marker in liver and is detectable down to 0.5 T per the pipeline.

Caveats / critique (12 points, 584 words) — Concentration 100 mM mobile-protein residue-equivalent is at the low end but defensible. Total liver protein is ~100-150 g/L (~600-900 mM residue-equivalent), b…
  • Concentration 100 mM mobile-protein residue-equivalent is at the low end but defensible. Total liver protein is ~100-150 g/L (~600-900 mM residue-equivalent), but only the mobile fraction (<~30 kDa, fast-tumbling) gives a sharp APT dip; the rest contributes to broadened MT. 10-20% of total protein by mass is in the mobile fraction, giving ~100-200 mM.
  • The 70-100 mM simulation range is reasonable. Species issue: in-vivo APT data (PMID 26334509) are from both Sprague-Dawley rats and humans; 3.5 ppm shift is consistent across species. No red flag on concentration. Backbone amide NH (amide class, 1H/residue, 3.5 ppm, intermediate exchange) -- all correct.
  • The 3.5 ppm shift is well-established in liver (PMID 36161668, 26334509, 26391991, 32785767 all use 3.5 ppm). The 100 mM effective pool is reasonable for the mobile fraction. Aliphatic C-H rNOE (rnoe class, 5 C-H/residue, -3.5 ppm) -- correct. 5 aliphatic C-H per residue is a reasonable average; -3.5 ppm is the standard mobile-protein rNOE position.
  • No exchangeable protons neglected: side-chain amides (Asn, Gln) are a small fraction and not separately resolved in the APT window. The chemist's identification of the two CEST-relevant pools (backbone amide + aliphatic rNOE) is complete and correct. APT amide: in-vivo human liver CEST consistently uses 3.5 ppm (PMID 36161668, 26334509, 26391991, 32785767). Simulation used 3.5 ppm. No discrepancy.
  • APT rNOE: -3.5 ppm is the standard in-vivo mobile-protein rNOE shift (8 references in provenance: brain, spinal cord, blood, kidney, stroke models). No liver-specific rNOE shift measurement exists in the cited literature, but -3.5 ppm is the universal class-level value. No discrepancy expected. None. Backbone amide (1H/residue) and aliphatic rNOE (5 C-H/residue) are the two CEST-relevant pools.
  • Side-chain amides and other exchangeable groups are present in individual residues but are a small fraction of the total pool and are not separately resolved in the APT CEST window. Robustness to input uncertainty: upper-bound only

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (amide NH2 (terminal C5 -C(=O)NH2) [amide]: concentration 7-20 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.02-0.24%, 1.5 T: 0.07-0.71%, 3 T: 0.09-1.35%, 5 T: 0.12-1.87%, 7 T: 0.14-2.06%. Threshold 0.5%. The point estimate is below threshold; only the high corner clears it.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • At all fields the simulated amide is at 3.5 ppm, 0 Hz from the APT pool (also 3.5 ppm) -- COMPLETE overlap with a ~10x larger competing pool (100 mM APT vs 7 mM glutamine). Additionally 0 Hz separation from APT means the glutamine amide is inseparable from APT by any extraction method.
  • If the true shift is 1.2 ppm (chemist's estimate), then there is no APT collision but there IS a collision with glycoCEST OH at ~1.0 ppm: 0.2 ppm gap = 10.7 Hz at 3 T, 28.6 Hz at 7 T, against a 5111 Hz linewidth -- total blur. Either way the glutamine amide is buried.
  • MT pool at -2.4 ppm is 754 Hz away at 3 T, linewidth 15950 Hz -- also blurred. No field provides a clean window for glutamine.

Direct water saturation:

  • Direct-saturation bandwidth 21.3 Hz (0.5-1.5 T), 31.9 Hz (3-7 T). Amide at 3.5 ppm is 150 Hz from water at 0.5 T, 451 Hz at 1.5 T, 902 Hz at 3 T, 1503 Hz at 5 T, 2105 Hz at 7 T -- all well clear of the direct-saturation band.
  • If the true shift is 1.2 ppm, the offset is 50 Hz at 0.5 T, 150 Hz at 1.5 T, 300 Hz at 3 T -- still clear. Direct saturation is not a problem for glutamine at any field. The problem is the APT or glycoCEST collision.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • Amide kex 65.5 s-1 is the median of two BRAIN-derived measurements (116 s-1 human brain, 15 s-1 in vivo n=7).
  • Provenance states 'no measurement of Glutamine's own amide protons -- a class-level amide value is used; no liver-specific exchange-rate measurement -- borrowed from brain, human.' This is a double borrow: wrong metabolite (peptide amide vs small-molecule terminal amide) AND wrong tissue (brain vs liver).
  • Small-molecule terminal amides exchange more slowly than peptide backbone amides; 65.5 s-1 may overestimate the glutamine-specific kex. The kex spread 15-158 s-1 brackets this. Amine group: NOT SIMULATED, UNKNOWN -- no reference value, no contrast can be claimed.

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • Swept B1 = 0.5-0.75 µT, Tsat = 0.75-3 s, sits in the slow-exchange regime. AREX or multi-pool Lorentzian fitting would be the methods of choice if the signal were large enough.
  • In reality, no extraction method can separate a 0.3% glutamine amide dip sitting at 0 Hz from a 2.3% APT dip (at 3.5 ppm) or from the glycoCEST OH window (at 1.2 ppm). The information is not in the Z-spectrum; no post-processing can recover it.
  • No literature citation establishes a method for detecting glutamine amide CEST in liver, because no such detection has been demonstrated.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

No verified disease application of this pool's CEST/NOE signal was found. Searched glutamine/gluCEST liver, glutamine CEST NOE, and liver glutamine MRS/metabolomics. No glutamine CEST/NOE study in liver (or brain CEST) found; glutamine MRS results found are brain (hepatic encephalopathy) and HCC tissue metabolomics. Dropped glutamine-glutamate (Glx)-combined and review-only hits lacking a direct glutamine measurement.

Caveats / critique (11 points, 506 words) — Concentration 7 mM free glutamine is a reasonable mid-range whole-liver estimate (free hepatic glutamine is ~1-10 mM depending on fasting state and compartment)…
  • Concentration 7 mM free glutamine is a reasonable mid-range whole-liver estimate (free hepatic glutamine is ~1-10 mM depending on fasting state and compartment). The 7-20 mM range is defensible. However, at 7 mM the per-molecule amide contrast is 0.07-0.48% across fields -- all below the 0.5% detectability threshold except marginally at 7 T.
  • Even at the 20 mM upper bound, 7 T contrast would be ~1.4%, but the APT overlap (if 3.5 ppm) or glycoCEST overlap (if 1.2 ppm) makes attribution impossible. Concentration is not the limiting factor; per-molecule contrast and spectral collision are.
  • Amide NH2 (terminal C5) -- class 'amide' is correct, BUT the chemist's own shift estimate is 1.2 ppm while the simulation used 3.5 ppm (the peptide-backbone-amide class value). This is the most consequential chemistry issue: a small-molecule terminal amide like glutamine's C5 -C(=O)NH2 resonates at ~1.0-1.5 ppm in solution (not H-bonded in a peptide chain), not at 3.5 ppm.
  • The simulated 3.5 ppm contrast is misattributed to the wrong frequency. If the true shift is ~1.2 ppm, the glutamine amide sits in the glycoCEST OH window, not at the APT position. Class is right, shift is wrong. Amine NH3+ (alpha) -- class 'amine' correct, correctly assessed as too fast-exchanging to be CEST-visible; marked NOT SIMULATED, UNKNOWN.
  • The chemist counted 2 labile protons; NH3+ actually has 3 exchangeable protons, but the practical conclusion (not CEST-visible) is unchanged. Hydroxyl placeholder correct (no OH, carboxylates deprotonated). No in-vivo liver CEST measurement of glutamine exists. The chemist's in-vitro/theoretical estimate is 1.2 ppm for the terminal amide, but the simulation used the class-level amide value of 3.5 ppm.
  • There is no in-vivo frequency to compare against; the discrepancy is between the chemist's own 1.2 ppm estimate and the 3.5 ppm that was simulated. If the true in-vivo shift is ~1.2 ppm, the glutamine amide collides with the glycoCEST OH window (~1.0 ppm) rather than with APT (3.5 ppm). None.
  • All exchangeable protons (terminal amide 2H, alpha-amine 3H, though amine is not CEST-visible) are accounted for. Carboxylates are deprotonated and contribute nothing.
  • Groups not simulated: amine NH3+ (alpha-amino, C1) [amine] -- the reference table has no verified exchange rate and shift for amine protons -- we don't know; not simulated; hydroxyl (none present; acid groups not exchangeable) [hydroxyl] -- the chemist judged this group not exchangeable with water; not simulated
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Chemist agent's proposed structure was WRONG and has been replaced with PubChem's verified structure for 'Glutamine'. Rejected SMILES: 'NCC(=O)N[C@@H](C(=O)O)CC(O)=O'; PubChem: 'C(CC(=O)N)[C@@H](C(=O)O)N'.
  • The exchangeable-proton groups below are still the chemist's own analysis and may have been reasoned from the wrong structure. Good 1H CEST candidate: glutamine has an amide (-CONH2) and a terminal alpha-amine (-NH3+) giving multiple exchangeable protons, with a CEST peak in the Gln/Glu region ~1.8-2.0 ppm (Gln/Glu group seen in 1H MRS, PMID 17128381, 11859290).
  • Concentration evidence is from animal (rat) perfused-liver/cell work, so animal_evidence_only=true.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial, centred on the portal-vein confluence / mid-upper abdomen (roughly L1-L2 level)

Why this scan:

  • An axial upper-abdominal slab at the portal-vein confluence cuts through the left hepatic lobe, both kidneys, the spleen, and the psoas muscle in one field of view. The candidate metabolites have sharply different tissue concentrations: hepatic glycogen is high and renal/muscle/splenic glycogen is low, and the mobile protein/peptide amide pool differs between liver, spleen (high cellularity), kidney, and muscle.
  • A single shared saturation sweep lets us test whether the ~0.5 ppm GlycoCEST dip and the 3.5 ppm APT dip scale with these known concentration differences across ROIs.
  • Generic MT/rNOE background is broadly similar across these soft tissues at a given offset, so a contrast that tracks the known concentration pattern (liver >> muscle at 0.5 ppm; spleen > liver for amide) is evidence of true metabolite exchange rather than generic background.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed rectangular train, B1=0.5 µT, 40 pulses × 60 ms (interpulse delay 40 ms, duty cycle 60%), total Tsat=4000 ms, TR=5000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): 0.5 µT mean B1 with a 60% duty cycle (2.4 s on out of a 5 s TR) gives a conservative specific absorption rate well within 3 T body-imaging limits (~1-2 W/kg average). The liver/kidney slab has no metal and the saturation is applied to a modest FOV, so SAR is comfortably feasible. The 1.3x B1 re-simulation (0.65 µT) also remains within limits.

Compromise rationale:

  • The physicist recommended 0.25 µT / 3000 ms for glycogen and 0.75 µT / 3000 ms for the amide pool. I adopt 0.5 µT / 4000 ms as a single compromise.
  • This slightly oversaturates the amide (favored, stronger and higher-shift pool, robust to the 0.7x B1 drop) and is modestly above the glycogen optimum but the long Tsat recovers the ~0.5 ppm OH dip.
  • The 0.7x/1.3x B1 sweep shows how much glycogen dip survives transmit inhomogeneity; a pure 0.25 µT would underdeliver on APT and a pure 0.75 µT would risk over-saturating and broadening the narrow OH peak.

Fat suppression: 2-point Dixon water-fat separation applied to the CEST readout (as validated in renal CEST, PMID 35476934). This anatomy is surrounded by perirenal, perisplenic, and perpancreatic fat and subcutaneous fat; near-0.5/1.0 ppm OH and NOE offsets are most vulnerable to fat-spectral contamination, and Dixon water-only images remove the fat peak without adding asymmetry. A SPIR/SPAIR prepulse alone is insufficient at these small offsets.

Motion mitigation: The scan uses navigator-gated (not breath-hold) respiratory gating so the long per-offset CEST acquisition stays synchronized to a quiet respiratory phase; a 5 s TR makes breath-holds impractical, so scan time is set by navigator acceptance (~15-25 min for the offset series). The abdominal viscera also require a steady feeding state (fed, not 12-h fasted) to keep hepatic glycogen high and reproducible; a brief fasting arm could be added later.

Slice coverage: Axial single slab, 20 mm thickness, centred on the portal-vein confluence (approximately L1-L2, ~1-2 cm below the xiphoid). The slab must contain the left hepatic lobe anteriorly, both kidneys at the hilum level, the splenic body posteriorly-laterally, the pancreatic body/tail, and the bilateral psoas muscles posteriorly. FOV ~40 cm, matrix ~256×256. One slab is sufficient; if the kidneys drop out, shift the slab 2 cm caudal and re-check all ROIs are present.

Structures in FOV: liver, spleen, renal cortex, pancreas, paraspinal muscle, stomach, aorta, inferior vena cava, subcutaneous fat

Z-spectrum sampling offsets:

  • -8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference (outside all pools)
  • -3.50 ppm: APT mirror (MTRasym), mobile protein aliphatic C-H rNOE, general lipid/membrane rNOE
  • -1.50 ppm: glycogen mirror reference
  • -1.00 ppm: glycoNOE dip, glycogen OH mirror
  • -0.50 ppm: Glycogen mirror reference (MTRasym)
  • +0.00 ppm: water (0 ppm), MT / rNOE baseline reference

  • +1.50 ppm: glycoCEST integrated band 0.5-1.5, glycoNOE tail

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, average the Z-spectrum over the ROI and compute MTRasym at each offset after B0 (WASSR) and B1 correction, with Dixon water-only images.
  • At the glycogen offsets (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 ppm and their negatives), test whether the MTRasym rank order matches the known glycogen ranking liver >> muscle > kidney > pancreas > spleen; a statistically significant liver-minus-muscle and liver-minus-spleen difference at 0.5-1.5 ppm that is NOT mirrored by an equal liver-minus-... difference at a far-off baseline (8 ppm) supports a glycogen-specific contribution.
  • At the amide offset (3.5 ppm and its -3.5 mirror), test whether spleen >= liver > kidney >= muscle, i.e. the cellular/splenic APT elevation; a spleen-minus-liver positive MTRasym at 3.5 ppm that does not appear at 8 ppm supports amide rather than generic MT.
  • Inconclusive if the ROI-to-ROI differences are comparable at the metabolite offset and at the far-off baseline (background-dominated) or if the ranking does not match the concentration ranking.

Not actively targeted: Glutamine was not actively designed around because the physicist agent reported no detectable simulated with-vs-without contrast for it at any field strength; its amine/amide contributions are subsumed into the broad 3.5 ppm amide band and it has no distinct resolvable offset in this compromise protocol.

Caveats:

  • Real limits for this anatomy: (1) ROI partial volume -- the renal cortex is a thin shell and the pancreatic body/tail can be small, so 20 mm slab + ~1.5 mm in-plane voxels risk mixing cortex/medulla and pancreas/fat; use the thinnest practical slice.
  • (2) B0/B1 inhomogeneity across the 40 cm FOV (air/bone at the spine, liver-rib interface) shifts the 0.5 and 3.5 ppm offsets differently per ROI even after WASSR; the 0.7x/1.3x B1 re-simulation bounds this. (3) Susceptibility from bowel gas (stomach/colon anterior) and the vertebral body distorts the Z-spectrum at low offsets, most affecting the 0.5 ppm glycogen dip.
  • (4) One compromise B1/Tsat cannot be simultaneously optimal for the narrow ~0.5 ppm OH (favoring low B1) and the broad 3.5 ppm amide (favoring higher B1); the 0.5 µT / 4 s choice is a middle ground and the glycogen dip may be undersaturated relative to its ideal.
  • (5) Glycogen is fasted-state sensitive, so subject feeding must be standardized or the liver-vs-muscle glycogen differential is unstable.
